chunks: And from him, from Abd al-Rahman, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from Aban ibn Taghlib, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who performed one or two circuits (shawt/shawtayn) of Tawaf, then left with a man for his need, he said: 'If it was a voluntary Tawaf, he builds upon it [completes the remaining circuits from where he left off], and if it was an obligatory Tawaf, he does not build upon it [must start over].'

key_terms.بَنَى عَلَيْهِ: He built upon it, meaning he continued from the point of interruption without restarting
key_terms.شَوْطًا: A circuit or round (singular of shawt)
key_terms.طَوَاف: Tawaf, the ritual circumambulation of the Kaaba

ai.seo_question: Does breaking Tawaf for a need invalidate the circuits already performed?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the juristic distinction between voluntary (nafl) and obligatory (fard) acts of worship regarding the validity of continuity (ittisal). It establishes that while minor interruptions in voluntary Tawaf do not invalidate the partial circuits, allowing the worshiper to resume from where they left off, the same leniency does not apply to obligatory Tawaf, which requires strict continuity from the start. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the higher standard of perfection required for obligatory rituals compared to voluntary ones.
